_readme: Edit text here, then rerun backend/scripts/build_featured.py. A card only appears on the Featured page once 'verified' is true, which a person sets after looking at the real frames. build_dets = detectors to pre-compute (the first is the default view).

cards.name: Barnard's Star
cards.title: Watch the star walk
cards.blurb: The fastest-moving star in our sky shifts about 10 arcseconds a year, almost two SPHEREx pixels. Blink between the first and latest survey and watch it step north while the stars behind it stay put.
cards.can_see: Its position, clearly. Not its brightness: the core is saturated (black), so brightness cannot be measured here.

cards.name: ε Indi B
cards.title: Same sky, different colours
cards.blurb: A pair of brown dwarfs, too cool to shine much in visible light. Compare detector 1 with detector 6: they get relatively brighter at longer infrared wavelengths, while ordinary stars fade.
cards.can_see: Colour differences between detectors. Their motion is subtle (under a pixel a year), and the two dwarfs are 0.6″ apart, so they appear as one dot. Their sun, ε Indi A, is in the same 20′ field.

cards.name: WISE 0855−0714
cards.title: The coldest known brown dwarf
cards.blurb: The coldest brown dwarf known, at roughly Earth-surface temperatures. If SPHEREx sees it at all, it will only be at 4–5 µm (detectors 5 and 6).
cards.can_see: Possibly nothing: it sits at the edge of what SPHEREx can detect in its first year. Look inside the dashed circle in detectors 5 and 6, and compare with detector 1, where it should be invisible.

cards.name: RW Aurigae
cards.title: Variable or saturated?
cards.blurb: A young star known for irregular dimming. Before trusting any brightness change, switch on the pixel tint: if its core is saturated, the change is not measurable here.
cards.can_see: Whether its core is usable in each detector. It lies near the ecliptic, so asteroids may cross the field in the Every-exposure view.

cards.name: R Draconis
cards.title: A pulsating giant near the pole
cards.blurb: A Mira variable that swells and fades over about 246 days. It lies near the north ecliptic pole, so SPHEREx visits it far more often than most of the sky.
cards.can_see: Many visits and strong colour differences between detectors. It is very bright, so expect saturation; brightness only means something where pixels are not flagged.

cards.name: North ecliptic pole deep field
cards.title: The most-visited patch of sky
cards.blurb: SPHEREx passes over the poles of the ecliptic on every orbit, so this patch has the longest timeline of all. Step through it survey by survey.
cards.can_see: Many epochs of the same faint galaxies and stars. Good for seeing what stays the same, which is most of the sky.

cards.name: Orion Nebula
cards.title: Dust and ices in Orion
cards.blurb: A nearby star-forming region. Detector 4 covers wavelengths where dust grains and ices glow or absorb, so the cloud looks very different from detector 1.
cards.can_see: Large-scale glowing dust and gas. The brightest stars are saturated.
